lesson.title: Main ideas and summaries
lesson.intro: Find the main point of the whole passage.

sections.heading: Match a summary to the passage’s full movement
body: Summarize the passage’s movement without listing every detail. In the map passage: initial interpretation → uneven participant pool → revised caption and wider participation.
A correct summary explains why all major paragraphs belong. Reject an option that omits a limitation, reverses the outcome, or focuses on one memorable example.

examples.text:
Passage A — Theater director
Our theater’s facade is intact, but the stage rigging is unsafe. Preserving the room exactly as it stood in 1930 would make it impossible to use. I want to retain the painted ceiling and the worn foyer steps while replacing the cables above the stage. A public building survives through repeated encounters. A locked theater is a photograph of itself.

Passage B — Architectural historian
Use can help preserve a theater, but “modernization” is sometimes a generous word for erasure. The original stage equipment reveals how productions were mounted; removing all of it would sever that record. I support new safety systems, provided representative old mechanisms remain visible and the alterations are documented. Preservation need not mean freezing a building. It means knowing what changes cost.

Both writers are responding to a proposed renovation. Neither disputes that the existing rigging is unsafe. The debate concerns how to change the theater while retaining what makes its past legible.

Question: Taken together, the passages chiefly examine:

Supported answer: how a theater can remain usable while preserving evidence of its history

Reason: Both writers accept safety changes and debate what should remain during renovation. The supported answer is “how a theater can remain usable while preserving evidence of its history.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.
examples.label: Worked example 2: Two Ways to Keep a Theater

activity.prompt: A curator first calls a map inaccurate, then learns that it records local memories rather than measured distances. Which summary follows that movement?
choices: The curator discovers a different purpose for the map
The curator accepts local memories as a substitute for measured distances
The curator concludes that a map is accurate whenever it records many memories
activity.explanation: The curator changes the question used to judge the map: it records memories rather than geographic distances. The map does not become a substitute for measured distances, and the passage gives no rule linking accuracy to the number of memories. Summarize the change in understanding, not a new fact about the object.

sections.heading: Reject narrow, inflated, and imported choices
body: Test three traps: a narrow choice covers only one detail; an inflated choice claims more than the passage; an imported choice adds an idea the text never develops.
Check who the answer includes and how sure it sounds. “The interviewed residents” is narrower than “everyone,” and “promising” is weaker than “proven.” Point to the words that support the choice.

examples.text:
A town introduced a Saturday bus between the library and three neighborhoods. Before the pilot, residents at public meetings had asked for daily service. The transport office could initially fund only eight Saturdays. It counted riders and invited anonymous comments after each trip.

The first Saturday drew twelve passengers. By the eighth, twenty-nine people rode. Several comments praised the library stop; others asked for an earlier departure. One resident wrote that the trip was useful but too infrequent for a weekday job. A council member called the growing attendance encouraging. The office’s report used a more guarded phrase: the figures supported continuing the trial, not yet expanding it to every day.

The report noted two limits. The trial took place during a summer reading program, and it did not measure how many riders would pay a fare. The office proposed another eight weeks after the program ended, with an optional fare question on the comment card. The council approved the additional trial without promising a permanent route.

Question: The passage’s main point is that the town:

Supported answer: is using a promising bus pilot to gather evidence before making a larger commitment

Reason: Rider numbers rise, but the report proposes further testing because demand under different conditions remains uncertain. The supported answer is “is using a promising bus pilot to gather evidence before making a larger commitment.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.
examples.label: Worked example 3: The Bus Pilot

activity.prompt: A passage describes increased weekend trips in a transit pilot, then argues that access improved while cost problems remain. Which choice is too narrow to summarize the whole passage?
choices: The pilot improves access but leaves its financial sustainability unsettled
Access gains make the pilot promising, while cost questions prevent a final verdict
activity.explanation: “Weekend trips increased” gives only a benefit and omits the unresolved costs. Both other summaries include an access gain and a financial qualification, so they can cover the whole argument. A detail can be accurate yet too narrow to serve as the main idea.

questions.subject: reading
questions.questionText: The passage primarily argues that the glacier’s dust bands:
choices: primarily record volcanic activity whose effects can be separated from the effects of summer warmth
are strongest as temperature measures when tree records agree, regardless of where the dust originated
can inform climate reconstruction when their sources and processes are considered alongside other evidence
date summer warmth more precisely than tree records through differences in mineral composition
questions.explanation: The researchers use the bands as contributing evidence while investigating dust sources, possible effects, and other records. Agreement with tree peaks does not make source irrelevant or improve dates beyond the stated precision. Most tested bands resemble valley material rather than volcanic deposits.

passage.title: The Dust between the Layers
passage.context:
A core removed from a mountain glacier contains thin bands of dark dust between layers of compressed snow. A team studying the core found several dust bands near layers whose chemistry suggested unusually warm summers. One account of the result described the dust as a “thermometer preserved in ice.” The phrase was vivid, but it collapsed several possible sequences into one.

Dust might have arrived during warm, dry weather that exposed bare ground downwind. It might also have arrived after an eruption or an unusually strong storm, neither of which required a warm summer at the glacier. Once deposited, dark material could absorb more sunlight than clean snow and contribute to melting. In that case, dust could be partly a consequence of regional conditions and partly an influence on the local ice surface. The possibilities were not exclusive.

To investigate the source, the team compared the bands’ mineral composition with samples from exposed valleys and volcanic deposits. Most bands more closely resembled valley material, but two had a different signature. The team also compared the sequence with nearby tree records that estimated summer warmth independently. Several broad peaks aligned; their dates were not precise enough to establish which event came first within a particular summer.

The researchers concluded that the dust bands could contribute to a reconstruction when interpreted alongside other evidence. They rejected using the darkness of a band as a direct reading of summer temperature. A pale layer did not prove a cold season, since ground cover and winds might have limited dust transport. A dark layer did not identify a single cause. The core preserved an intersection of processes, not a set of labels waiting to be read aloud.

reviewQuestions.subject: reading
reviewQuestions.questionText: The passage’s central point is that:
choices: claims of service growth depend on which measure and comparison base are used
annual identifier resetting explains why the share of households using the centers declined
visits provide a more useful measure of household access than population estimates do
the centers’ increased workload indicates that residents’ unresolved needs became more complex
reviewQuestions.explanation: Visits and household totals rise while the proportion falls because the service-area estimate rises faster. The claim therefore depends on its measure and denominator. Resetting identifiers limits cross-year identification, not the annual share calculation. The table does not compare usefulness of measures or complexity of residents’ needs.

passage.title: A Changing Denominator
passage.context:
A city’s annual report announced that use of its neighborhood advice centers had increased. The statement was true in one sense: the centers recorded more visits. The report also said that “a growing proportion of local households is receiving help.” That second claim required information the visit totals did not supply.

The accompanying table separates visits, distinct households recorded as visiting, and households estimated to live in the service area. Staff assigned each visiting household an anonymous identifier, so repeat visits could be distinguished from first visits within a year. The identifiers were reset at the start of the next year, meaning the table could not show which households returned from one year to the next.

A researcher, Oren, noted that the share of households recorded as visiting had actually declined, even though both visits and distinct visiting households had risen. New housing had expanded the estimated service-area population more rapidly. The centers had served more households in absolute terms while reaching a smaller share of the enlarged population.

This did not establish that residents found the service less helpful. The table included no measure of satisfaction, whether a problem was resolved, or how many households needed advice. Nor did it show that any specific household had lost access. Oren recommended keeping the original statement about visits, replacing the proportional claim, and adding a separate study of unmet need. “The denominator is not an inconvenience,” he wrote. “It is part of the question.” The revised report retained all three columns rather than choosing the one that made the largest increase appear.

reviewQuestions.subject: reading
reviewQuestions.questionText: The passages chiefly debate:
choices: which individual merchant first named the riverside landing
whether the petition map exists in more than one surviving copy
whether an uncertain legal claim leaves room for evidence of shared practical use
how to determine the map’s exact scale from the ferry queue
reviewQuestions.explanation: A cautions against inferring established rights from an advocacy document. B accepts that caution but argues for practical-use evidence. The disagreement concerns what can still be learned, not the map’s scale, number of copies, or individual namer.

passage.title: The Map in the Petition
passage.context:
Passage A — Historical geographer
A map attached to an 1810 petition shades a narrow strip beside the river and labels it “common landing.” Later historians have used the map to show that the landing belonged to everyone in the district. The petition’s authors were merchants seeking a road to the river. Their map certainly shows that they wanted officials to recognize a shared landing. It does not, by itself, establish an uncontested legal right. A petition presents a case. We should examine the records of neighboring landholders and the authorities’ response before turning its desired recognition into an accomplished fact.

Passage B — Historian of everyday commerce
The warning about legal title is sound, but it should not reduce the map to evidence of an unrealized wish. Merchants built an argument around a place that their readers were expected to recognize. The map locates warehouses, a ferry queue, and a route worn between them. Those details may reveal a shared working geography even if formal rights were disputed. I would compare the map with delivery records and references to tolls. Such evidence could tell us how people used the landing while the question of ownership remained unsettled. A place can function as common ground without being common property.

The surviving map does not name individual users. No official response to the petition has yet been located. Both historians distinguish the document’s claim from a final legal determination.

Oren recommended keeping the original statement about visits, replacing the proportional claim, and adding a separate study of unmet need. “The denominator is not an inconvenience,” he wrote. “It is part of the question.” The revised report retained all three columns rather than choosing the one that made the largest increase appear.

questions.subject: reading
questions.questionText: The passages chiefly debate:
choices: which individual merchant first named the riverside landing
whether the petition map exists in more than one surviving copy
whether an uncertain legal claim leaves room for evidence of shared practical use
how to determine the map’s exact scale from the ferry queue
questions.explanation: A cautions against inferring established rights from an advocacy document. B accepts that caution but argues for practical-use evidence. The disagreement concerns what can still be learned, not the map’s scale, number of copies, or individual namer.

passage.title: The Map in the Petition
passage.context:
Passage A — Historical geographer
A map attached to an 1810 petition shades a narrow strip beside the river and labels it “common landing.” Later historians have used the map to show that the landing belonged to everyone in the district. The petition’s authors were merchants seeking a road to the river. Their map certainly shows that they wanted officials to recognize a shared landing. It does not, by itself, establish an uncontested legal right. A petition presents a case. We should examine the records of neighboring landholders and the authorities’ response before turning its desired recognition into an accomplished fact.

Passage B — Historian of everyday commerce
The warning about legal title is sound, but it should not reduce the map to evidence of an unrealized wish. Merchants built an argument around a place that their readers were expected to recognize. The map locates warehouses, a ferry queue, and a route worn between them. Those details may reveal a shared working geography even if formal rights were disputed. I would compare the map with delivery records and references to tolls. Such evidence could tell us how people used the landing while the question of ownership remained unsettled. A place can function as common ground without being common property.

The surviving map does not name individual users. No official response to the petition has yet been located. Both historians distinguish the document’s claim from a final legal determination.

lesson.title: Geometry
lesson.intro: Use shapes, angles, and measurements to find missing values.

sections.heading: 1. Translate the diagram and protect units
body: Mark the given measurements and the requested quantity. Height must meet the base at a right angle; a slanted side is not the height. Areas: triangle \(\frac{bh}{2}\), parallelogram \(bh\), trapezoid \(\frac{(b_1+b_2)h}{2}\).
Convert mixed units before calculating. Length uses units such as cm; area uses cm²; volume uses cm³. If a shape is built from several pieces, add what is included and subtract what is removed.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: A 10-by-7 rectangle has a radius-3 quarter-circle removed from a corner. The rectangle contributes 70 square units; the removed region is \(\pi(3^2)/4=9\pi/4\). Remaining area is \(70-9\pi/4\), approximately 62.93, which is smaller than the full rectangle.

sections.tip: Write the intended units next to your target before inserting numbers.

activity.prompt: A trapezoid has parallel bases 6 and 18, perpendicular height 4, and a slanted side 7. Which setup gives its area?
activity.explanation: Average the two parallel bases, then multiply by the perpendicular height: (6+18)×4/2=48 square units. Using 7 substitutes a slanted side for the height; using only the larger base treats the trapezoid as a rectangle.

sections.heading: 2. Triangles: heights, angles, and allowed sides
body: For a right triangle, find the hypotenuse—the side opposite the right angle— and use \(a^2+b^2=c^2\). Recognize side lengths 3–4–5, 5–12–13, and 8–15–17, including sets multiplied by the same number. Special triangles have sides \(x,x,x\sqrt2\) for 45–45–90 and \(x,x\sqrt3,2x\) for 30–60–90; confirm the angles first.

A triangle’s third side must be longer than the difference of the other two and shorter than their sum: \(|a-b|<x<a+b\). A line splitting an angle in half divides the opposite side in the ratio of the two sides touching that angle, not always equally.

With three known sides, Heron’s formula gives area \(\sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}\), where \(s=\frac{a+b+c}{2}\). For sides 5,5,6, s=8 and area=√(8·3·3·2)=12. The altitude to the 6-unit base is 4, independently confirming area 6·4/2=12.

A regular polygon has equal sides and angles. With n sides, each interior angle (inside angle) is \(\frac{180(n-2)}n\) degrees and each outside (exterior) angle is \(\frac{360}n\) degrees. Exterior angles sum to 360 degrees.

Parallel lines cut by a transversal have equal corresponding and alternate interior angles; same-side interior angles sum to 180°. A triangle’s angles sum to 180°, and equal sides face equal angles. If two equal angles are each x and the third is 40°, then 2x+40=180 gives x=70°. Triangles are congruent under SSS, SAS, ASA/AAS, or right-triangle hypotenuse-leg; equal angles alone establish similarity, not equal size. A rectangle has two reflection axes; a nonsquare rhombus has its two diagonals as axes; a general parallelogram has half-turn symmetry but no reflection axis.

A median joins a vertex to the opposite midpoint; the three medians meet at the centroid, which is 2/3 of each median from the vertex. In coordinates it is \((\frac{x_1+x_2+x_3}3,\frac{y_1+y_2+y_3}3)\). The incenter is the intersection of angle bisectors, not medians: its radius is r=area/semiperimeter. A right triangle with legs 5,12 has hypotenuse 13, area 30, semiperimeter 15, and inradius 2. Its circumcenter is the hypotenuse midpoint, with circumradius 13/2. Keep the centers and radii distinct.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: An equilateral triangle of side 8 has altitude 4√3, found from a right triangle with hypotenuse 8 and short leg 4. Its area is \(8(4\sqrt3)/2=16\sqrt3\). For sides 6,11 and integer x, the strict triangle interval 5<x<17 gives eleven values, 6 through 16.

sections.tip: Check that a claimed hypotenuse is the longest side and that triangle endpoints are excluded.

activity.prompt: A triangle has sides 4 and 9. Which third side is possible?
activity.explanation: The third side must be strictly between 9 − 4 = 5 and 9 + 4 = 13. Equality makes a flat, degenerate triangle.

sections.heading: 4. Circle angles, chords, tangents, and secants
body: An arc is part of a circle’s edge. Find the arc between the angle’s arms. An angle at the center equals the arc’s angle measure; an angle on the edge is half as large. A tangent touches the circle once, at a right angle to the radius. A chord joins two edge points; a line from the center meeting it at 90° cuts it in half.

A secant crosses the circle at two points. Multiply the right lengths: crossing chords give part × part on each chord; two secants from an outside point give outside part × whole length; tangent and secant give \(\text{tangent}^2=\text{external}\times\text{whole}\). Add outside and inside portions to get the whole secant.

For θ in degrees, arc length is \(\frac\theta{360}\times2\pi r\). Radius 12 and angle 75° give \(\frac{75}{360}\times24\pi=5\pi\). Arc measure is an angle; arc length is a distance. A complete circumference supplies a useful upper bound.

Tangents and half-chords form right triangles. Radius 8 and center-to-external-point distance 17 give tangent √(17²−8²)=15. Radius 10 and center-to-chord distance 8 give half-chord 6, so the chord is 12. The radius to a tangency point is perpendicular to the tangent, while the center’s perpendicular bisects a chord.

For θ in degrees, a sector has area \(\frac\theta{360}\pi r^2\). In radians, arc length is \(r\theta\) and sector area is \(\frac12r^2\theta\). For radius 6 and angle \(\pi/3\), arc length is \(2\pi\) and sector area is \(6\pi\); one is a length and the other an area.

Opposite angles in a quadrilateral with all vertices on a circle sum to 180°: an angle of 112° forces its opposite to be 68°. For angles formed by two chords crossing inside, use half the sum of intercepted opposite arcs. For an angle outside formed by two secants or tangents, use half the difference of the intercepted arcs. A tangent-chord angle has half its intercepted arc. First locate the angle’s vertex; this determines which rule applies.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: A radius-17 circle has a chord 8 units from its center. Half the chord is \(\sqrt{17^2-8^2}=15\), so the chord is 30. For a tangent and secant with outside segment 5 and inside segment 4, the whole is 9: tangent²=5(9)=45 and tangent=3√5. Distinguish half, inside, and whole lengths.

sections.tip: Draw brackets for outside, inside, and whole segments before multiplying.

activity.prompt: An inscribed angle intercepts a 96° arc. What is the angle?
activity.explanation: The vertex is on the circle, so the angle is half its intercepted arc: 96°/2=48°. The 96° option would be the corresponding central angle; 192° reverses the half-arc relationship.

sections.heading: 5. Coordinates and vectors as geometric tools
body: Between \((x_1,y_1)\) and \((x_2,y_2)\), distance is \(\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}\). For the point halfway between them, average the x-values and then the y-values. A missing endpoint is twice the midpoint minus the known endpoint. Put negative coordinates in parentheses.

Slope is change in y divided by change in x. Parallel lines run in the same direction and share slopes. Lines at right angles have slopes that multiply to −1, unless one line is vertical. Handle horizontal and vertical lines separately. For area, look for a horizontal or vertical base with an easy height at a right angle to the base.

The shortest, perpendicular distance from \((x_0,y_0)\) to \(Ax+By+C=0\) is \(\frac{|Ax_0+By_0+C|}{\sqrt{A^2+B^2}}\). Put zero on the right first. From the origin to \(3x+4y=20\), distance is \(\frac{|-20|}{\sqrt{3^2+4^2}}=4\).

A circle has equation \((x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2\). Complete the square in both coordinates: \(x^2+y^2+4x-10y+20=0\) becomes \((x+2)^2+(y-5)^2=9\), with center (−2,5) and radius 3. For rotations about the origin: 90° counterclockwise sends \((x,y)\to(-y,x)\); 180° sends \((-x,-y)\); 90° clockwise sends \((y,-x)\). For another center, subtract its coordinates, rotate, then add them back.

Reflect across the x-axis using \((x,-y)\), the y-axis using \((-x,y)\), or \(y=x\) using \((y,x)\). Across \(x=h\), use \((2h-x,y)\). Thus reflecting (7,1) across x=2 gives (−3,1). A dilation centered at (h,k) multiplies the displacement from that center by the scale factor.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: If A=(−3,8) and midpoint M=(2,1), the other endpoint is B=2M−A=(7,−6); averaging A and B recovers M. Vectors (5,1) and (−2,4) span a parallelogram of area |5·4−1(−2)|=22, using perpendicular height rather than multiplying slanted side lengths.

sections.tip: Use coordinate differences and perpendicular heights instead of measuring the sketch.

activity.prompt: A segment has endpoints (−2, 3) and (4, 11). Which calculation gives its length?
activity.explanation: Subtract corresponding coordinates first: Δx = 6 and Δy = 8. Distance is the hypotenuse of that reference triangle, so the length is 10.

questions.subject: math
questions.stem: A triangle has side lengths 13, 14, and 15.
questions.questionText: What is its area?
questions.explanation: The semiperimeter is \(s = \frac{13+14+15}{2} = 21\). Heron’s formula gives \(A = \sqrt{21\times8\times7\times6} = \sqrt{7056} = 84\). As a geometric check, the altitude to the 14-unit base is 12, so \(A = 14 \times  \frac{12}{2}\). Treating 13 or 15 as a perpendicular height is the trap.

lesson.title: Geometry
lesson.intro: Use shapes, angles, and measurements to find missing values.

sections.heading: 3. Similarity across lengths, areas, and volumes
body: Match sides in the same position using labels and equal angles. If the larger-to-smaller length factor is k, the distance around each shape multiplies by k, areas multiply by \(k^2\), and volumes multiply by \(k^3\). Do not use an area ratio directly as a side ratio.

Find the multiplier for side lengths with the square root of an area ratio or cube root of a volume ratio. Turning or flipping a shape does not change these ratios. Label drawing and actual measurements before writing a scale ratio.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: Similar triangles with areas 16 and 49 have length ratio 4:7. A smaller perimeter of 20 therefore becomes 35. Similar solids with lengths in ratio 2:5 and smaller volume 24 have larger volume \(24(5/2)^3=375\); the volume multiplier is 125/8, not 5/2.

sections.tip: Before applying a scale factor, say length, area, or volume and choose exponent 1, 2, or 3.

activity.prompt: Two solids are similar. The larger has 1.5 times every corresponding length. The smaller volume is 16 cubic units. What is the larger volume?
activity.explanation: The volume multiplier is the cube of the length factor: 1.5³=3.375. Thus volume is 16×3.375=54 cubic units. Multiplying by 1.5 gives 24 and applies length scaling; multiplying by 1.5² gives 36 and applies area scaling.

questions.subject: math
questions.stem: Two similar triangles have areas in the ratio 9:25. The smaller triangle has perimeter 18.
questions.questionText: What is the larger triangle’s perimeter?
questions.explanation: Area scales with the square of the side-length factor. The smaller-to-larger length ratio is \(\sqrt{\frac{9}{25}} = \frac{3}{5}\). Perimeter scales like length, so the larger perimeter is \(18\left(\frac53\right)=30\). Applying the area ratio directly to perimeter would give 50.

reviewQuestions.subject: math
reviewQuestions.stem: A circle has center O and radius 10. Chord AB has length 16 and midpoint M. Point P lies on the ray from O through M, beyond the circle, with OP=26.
reviewQuestions.questionText: What is the area of triangle PAB?
reviewQuestions.explanation: OM is perpendicular to AB and bisects it, so AM=8 and OM=√(10²−8²)=6. Because P lies beyond M on the named ray, its perpendicular distance to line AB is PM=26−6=20. Triangle PAB has base 16 and height 20, giving area 16(20)/2=160. Using OP=26 as the height measures from the center instead of the chord.

reviewQuestions.subject: math
reviewQuestions.stem: Two similar solids have volumes in the ratio 8:27.
reviewQuestions.questionText: What is the ratio of their corresponding lengths, smaller to larger?
reviewQuestions.explanation: Volume scales with the cube of the length factor. Taking cube roots gives the corresponding length ratio ∛8:∛\(27 = 2:3\). Squaring that ratio would describe surface areas, while reversing it would compare the larger solid to the smaller one.

lesson.title: Read the evidence before the choices
lesson.intro: Find the right value in a table or graph.

sections.heading: Locate the quantity and unit
body: Name the quantity requested, its unit, and the treatment or time. Match the table column or graph axis before comparing values. In a graph, use the legend to select the correct series.
A final amount, a change, and a rate answer different questions. Reading the largest number without its label can select the wrong quantity.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For the lowest outlet dust, compare 6, 3, and 9 mg/m³: choose Vent Y. Its 45 m³/min airflow answers a different question.

activity.prompt: A thermometer table lists elapsed time and temperature. Which column answers “how warm at 4 min”?
activity.explanation: The question asks for temperature at a specified time. Time selects the row; temperature is the requested output.
activity.evidenceText: Trial 1: at 4 min the sample is 32°C and has volume 50 mL.

evidence.title: Locate the quantity and unit
evidence.context: Three air filters were tested under the same inlet dust concentration. The table separates outlet dust from airflow.

sections.heading: Distinguish totals, changes, and fractions
body: Change = final − initial. Amount removed = initial − final. Fraction removed divides the removed amount by the initial amount; fraction remaining divides the final amount by the initial amount.
Percentage-point change subtracts percentages. Relative percent change divides that difference by the original percentage. A rate additionally divides a change by elapsed time.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: Water treatment changes concentration from 60 to 15 mg/L. Removed = 45 mg/L; removed fraction = 45/60 = 75%; remaining fraction = 25%.

activity.prompt: A sample falls from 50 to 20 mg/L. What percentage of its initial concentration was removed?
activity.explanation: Removal is 50−20 = 30 mg/L. Divide by the initial 50, not the remaining 20: 30/50 = 60%.
activity.evidenceText: Concentration: initial 50 mg/L; final 20 mg/L; volume unchanged.

evidence.title: Distinguish totals, changes, and fractions
evidence.context: A treatment starts with 60 mg/L solute and finishes with 15 mg/L; water volume is unchanged.

questions.subject: science
questions.stem: What fraction of the initial suspended solids did Filter P remove?
questions.questionText: What fraction of the initial suspended solids did Filter P remove?
questions.explanation: P reduced solids from 40 to 8 mg/L, removing 32 mg/L. The removed fraction is 32/40 = 4/5.

passage.title: Filtering reservoir water
passage.context: Researchers passed separate 1 L samples of reservoir water through three filters. They measured suspended solids before and after filtration. Each sample was collected at the same depth; values are means of three trials. Lower solids after filtration mean clearer water.

questions.subject: science
questions.stem: Which standards have retention factors matching the unknown’s two bands?
questions.questionText: Which standards have retention factors matching the unknown’s two bands?
questions.explanation: Unknown bands are at 18 and 48 mm with a 60 mm front, matching C’s 0.30 and E’s 0.80. The data suggest two possible components.

passage.title: Separating dissolved pigments
passage.context: A solution was spotted at a pencil origin on paper. The paper stood in solvent, which moved upward. Each standard pigment was run separately with a solvent front 60 mm above the origin. The unknown produced two distinct colored bands. Retention factor Rf is band distance divided by solvent-front distance; the investigators treated matching Rf values as evidence of a possible match, not proof of chemical identity.

questions.subject: science
questions.stem: Which statement is supported by the unknown’s measurements?

The unknown definitely contains only C and E because its bands match their retention factors.

The unknown’s two observed bands traveled different fractions of the solvent-front distance.

sections.heading: Check simultaneous constraints
body: Turn every requirement into a separate test. “At least” includes equality; “greater than” does not. Eliminate a candidate as soon as it fails a required condition.
Write ratios in the requested direction. Output per area means output/area. Reversing numerator and denominator changes both the units and the ranking.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: Need airflow ≥70 m³/min and outlet dust ≤7 mg/m³. X passes both (80, 6); Y fails airflow; Z fails dust.

activity.prompt: Which water sample meets BOTH temperature below 25°C and oxygen at least 6 mg/L?
activity.explanation: M has 24°C and 6 mg/L and passes both. N fails the strict temperature limit; O fails the oxygen minimum.

evidence.title: Check simultaneous constraints
evidence.context: Use the same three air filters; the specification requires both sufficient airflow and sufficiently low outlet dust.

sections.heading: Normalize unequal sample sizes
body: Counts measure totals; densities measure counts per area or volume. Divide before ranking samples of unequal sizes. If every sample has the same size, counts and densities rank them alike.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: Quadrat A: 36/6 = 6 plants/m². B: 45/15 = 3 plants/m². B has the larger count, but A has the greater density.

activity.prompt: Which pool has the greater insect density?
activity.explanation: U has 24/3 = 8 insects/L; V has 30/6 = 5 insects/L. Dividing by volume makes the samples comparable.
activity.evidenceText: U: 24 insects in 3 L. V: 30 insects in 6 L.

evidence.title: Normalize unequal sample sizes
evidence.context: Two differently sized quadrats were surveyed using the same counting method.

sections.heading: Locate the quantity and unit
body: Name the quantity requested, its unit, and the treatment or time. Match the table column or graph axis before comparing values. In a graph, use the legend to select the correct series.
A final amount, a change, and a rate answer different questions. Reading the largest number without its label can select the wrong quantity.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For the lowest outlet dust, compare 6, 3, and 9 mg/m³: choose Vent Y. Its 45 m³/min airflow answers a different question.

activity.prompt: A thermometer table lists elapsed time and temperature. Which column answers “how warm at 4 min”?
activity.explanation: The question asks for temperature at a specified time. Time selects the row; temperature is the requested output.
activity.evidenceText: Trial 1: at 4 min the sample is 32°C and has volume 50 mL.

evidence.title: Locate the quantity and unit
evidence.context: Three air filters were tested under the same inlet dust concentration. The table separates outlet dust from airflow.

sections.heading: Distinguish totals, changes, and fractions
body: Change = final − initial. Amount removed = initial − final. Fraction removed divides the removed amount by the initial amount; fraction remaining divides the final amount by the initial amount.
Percentage-point change subtracts percentages. Relative percent change divides that difference by the original percentage. A rate additionally divides a change by elapsed time.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: Water treatment changes concentration from 60 to 15 mg/L. Removed = 45 mg/L; removed fraction = 45/60 = 75%; remaining fraction = 25%.

activity.prompt: A sample falls from 50 to 20 mg/L. What percentage of its initial concentration was removed?
activity.explanation: Removal is 50−20 = 30 mg/L. Divide by the initial 50, not the remaining 20: 30/50 = 60%.
activity.evidenceText: Concentration: initial 50 mg/L; final 20 mg/L; volume unchanged.

evidence.title: Distinguish totals, changes, and fractions
evidence.context: A treatment starts with 60 mg/L solute and finishes with 15 mg/L; water volume is unchanged.

lesson.title: Sentence Structure
lesson.intro: Build complete sentences and join their ideas correctly.

sections.heading: Clauses and phrases
body: A clause has a subject (who or what it is about) and a verb (an action or state, such as runs or is). An independent clause is a complete thought that can stand alone. A dependent clause needs another clause to finish its thought; it often starts with because, although, if, when, or while.

A phrase is a group of words without a complete subject and verb. Find those two parts first. If removing a starter such as because leaves a complete thought, you had a dependent clause. Do not decide only by where you pause.

examples.text: The excited child opened his present.
examples.label: Independent clause — you can stop here

examples.text: When the excited child opened his present…
examples.label: Dependent clause — the opening word forces you to keep going

examples.text: Excited to open his present…
examples.label: Phrase — no subject doing the action

sections.tip: Read it aloud. If you can stop talking, it is an independent clause. If you feel forced to keep going, it is dependent or a phrase.

questions.stem: Although the museum closes at six
questions.questionText: What kind of word group is this?
questions.explanation: “The museum” is the subject and “closes” is the verb. “Although” makes the thought dependent: we still need the main statement. Without “Although,” “The museum closes at six” can stand alone.
questions.subject: english

questions.questionText: Which word group is a phrase rather than a clause?
questions.explanation: “Near the old stone bridge” has no subject performing a verb. The other three groups each contain a subject and a verb; “While the river rose” is a dependent clause.
questions.subject: english

questions.stem: Even though the trail was muddy
questions.questionText: Which change makes this word group an independent clause?
questions.explanation: Removing the entire two-word starter “Even though” leaves “The trail was muddy,” a complete thought with subject “trail” and verb “was.” Removing the subject or the verb does not create an independent clause.
questions.subject: english

questions.questionText: Which word group is a dependent clause?
choices: Before the crew repaired the roof
questions.explanation: “Before” makes “the crew repaired the roof” dependent. It supplies a subject and working verb but leaves the reader waiting for a main statement. The first choice is independent; the other two are phrases.
questions.subject: english

lesson.title: Sentence Structure
lesson.intro: Build complete sentences and join their ideas correctly.

sections.heading: Sentence fragments
body: Read the entire sentence. It needs a subject, a main verb, and a complete thought; a fragment is missing one of these.
“The student running to class” has no main verb. Add one: “The student running to class dropped her bottle.” An -ed form can be either a past-tense verb or a modifier, so check its job.

examples.text: My little brother Shaun is excited to go to the beach and surf.
examples.label: Complete — has a subject and a working verb

examples.text: Excited to go to the beach and surf.
examples.label: Fragment — no subject

sections.tip: An -ing form needs a helping verb to serve as the main verb. An -ed form may be a past-tense verb or a modifier; check its job in the complete sentence.

questions.stem: The athlete training before sunrise.
questions.questionText: Which revision makes a complete sentence?
choices: The athlete to train before sunrise
questions.explanation: “Trained” supplies a working main verb for the subject “athlete.” “Training” and “to train” do not work as the main verb in these choices. The phrase “Training before sunrise” also lacks a subject.
questions.subject: english

questions.stem: The sculpture standing in the courtyard.
questions.questionText: Which revision supplies a working main verb?
choices: The sculpture standing in the courtyard
The sculpture standing in the courtyard attracts visitors
questions.explanation: “The sculpture” is the subject and “attracts” is the working main verb. “Standing in the courtyard” describes the sculpture but does not supply its main verb. The other choices still lack a subject or a working main verb.
questions.subject: english

questions.questionText: Which revision supplies the missing subject?
choices: The climbers reached the summit before noon
To reach the summit before noon
questions.explanation: “The climbers” supplies the subject for the working verb “reached.” The first choice lacks a subject; “Reaching” and “To reach” are not working main verbs in the other fragments.
questions.subject: english

reviewQuestions.questionText: Which word group is an independent clause?
reviewQuestions.explanation: “The musicians” is a subject and “packed” is a working verb. The thought is complete. “After” and “Because” make the other clauses dependent. “Carrying the heavy instrument” lacks a subject doing a working verb.
reviewQuestions.subject: english

reviewQuestions.questionText: Which choice is a complete sentence?
choices: The student excited to enter the competition
The student was excited to enter the competition
reviewQuestions.explanation: “The student” is the subject and “was” is the working verb. The other choices omit either the subject or a working main verb. Describing someone as “excited” does not supply the missing verb by itself.
reviewQuestions.subject: english

blocks.subject: reading

units.title: Evidence-based inference: Use the contradiction test on tempting options

lesson.title: Evidence-based inference
lesson.intro: Use clues in the passage to reach a supported conclusion.

sections.heading: Use the contradiction test on tempting options
body: For each remaining choice, ask what would have to be true. Then look for a passage detail that supports or contradicts that requirement.
Approving another trial does not promise permanent service. A choice that preserves uncertainty can fit better than one that sounds decisive.

examples.text:
Nico spent the first morning of the sound workshop recording traffic. The instructor asked him to choose a location and listen there for ten minutes before touching the recorder. He picked the bridge because he knew what he would hear: engines, tires, horns. He pressed the recording button after less than a minute.

When the instructor played his clip, the traffic filled every second. “You found what you expected,” she said. She sent him back without suggesting a different location. This time Nico stayed under the bridge. He noticed water striking a loose piece of timber, a bicycle chain clicking above him, and pauses in which the river seemed louder than the road. He began recording only after the ten minutes had passed.

That afternoon he compared the clips. The second still contained engines; listening had not removed them. But it also held the soft intervals he had missed. He labeled the first file “Bridge” and hesitated over the second. Finally he gave both files the same name and added only the dates. The place had not changed enough to explain the difference.

Question: Why does Nico give both files the same place name?

Supported answer: He recognizes that his attention, rather than a different location, explains the contrast

Reason: The last sentence states that the place had not changed enough to explain the difference. The supported answer is “He recognizes that his attention, rather than a different location, explains the contrast.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.
examples.label: Worked example 4: Listening Beneath the Bridge

activity.prompt: The text says, “Some residents welcomed the change; others remained skeptical.” Which inference fails the contradiction test?
activity.explanation: “Others remained skeptical” directly conflicts with universal support. Use explicit counterevidence to eliminate an attractive overstatement.

sections.heading: Pace a decision instead of rereading everything
body: Link a clue to your conclusion: “The text says __, so I can reasonably conclude __.” The better answer should require fewer details you have to invent.
If neither choice has a clear link, return to the relevant action or contrast instead of inventing an explanation.

activity.prompt: Which detail most directly supports the inference that the coach accepts Leah’s different portrayal of him?
choices: He mentions championships when Leah asks
The trophy cabinet appears at the far edge
He asks to keep the pencil lines around the unfinished tile
activity.explanation: His request retains the portrait’s focus on work rather than trophies. It is an action supporting acceptance; his earlier comment about the cabinet expresses a reservation.

evidence.title: The Unfinished Portrait
evidence.context:
Leah asked him instead to keep working while she made several sketches. He told her about a student who had returned years later to say that the team had been the first place she felt useful. He mentioned championships only when Leah asked. Her sketches showed his hands above the tile, one hand steadying it while the other tested the corner.

In the finished portrait, the trophy cabinet appeared at the far edge. The coach objected mildly that anyone looking for the championship would have to search. Leah said that anyone looking for him would not. The coach considered the canvas, then asked whether she could leave the pencil lines around the unfinished tile visible. She had planned to cover them. She agreed to let them remain.

sections.heading: Review the reason for the miss and test the repair
body: After a miss, name the unsupported leap: motive, certainty, future outcome, or a claim about everyone.
Replace it with a smaller conclusion and cite the action or statement that supports it. Try the same process on new text.

activity.prompt: An inference says Luis now finds the front entrance useless. What is the smallest supported correction?
choices: He values the side path’s encounters while still using the front steps for quick errands
He chooses the side path because it has become the quicker route
He uses the side path only when his father needs a route without steps
activity.explanation: The paragraph explicitly keeps the front entrance useful and the side path longer. Luis sometimes chooses the side path alone because his experience of it has changed.

evidence.title: The Second Entrance
evidence.context: When his father recovered, Luis used the front steps again for quick errands. But he sometimes chose the side path alone. It had not become shorter, and the front entrance had not become less useful. The route he had called inconvenient now held encounters he would otherwise have missed. He stopped referring to the doors as the usual entrance and the other one.

questions.subject: reading
questions.questionText: The author would most likely consider a transcript that silently presents the actor’s pauses as the poet’s instructions:
choices: preferable to page images because it eliminates uncertainty
misleading because it conceals the source of an interpretive decision
adequate because audio necessarily reproduces all visible marks exactly
irrelevant because no listener could compare a transcript with a reading
questions.explanation: The released transcript distinguishes speech from manuscript marks so readers do not attribute every pause to the poet. A silent conflation would remove that transparency, contrary to the rationale. Neither exact reproduction nor elimination of uncertainty is claimed.

passage.title: Hearing the Pause
passage.context:
A small publisher planned a spoken edition of a poet’s early notebooks. The notebooks include crossed-out words, incomplete lines, and spaces that may represent pauses or simply the end of a day’s writing. The producer wanted an actor to read the surviving words smoothly. A scholar proposed announcing each deletion and interruption. Both said they wanted listeners to encounter the notebooks rather than a finished poem that the poet had never written.

During a trial recording, the actor read one page twice. In the first version, she omitted the crossed-out words and connected a fragment to the next line. units.title: Words in context: Read the local meaning before recalling the dictionary

lesson.title: Words in context
lesson.intro: Use the surrounding sentence to work out a word’s meaning.

sections.heading: Use the screen to build a passage map
body: Locate the target word, then read its sentence and the sentences around it. Note what the word describes or acts on.
Your task is its meaning here. A familiar dictionary meaning can be wrong in this context.

activity.prompt: As used here, “clues” most nearly means:
choices: findings that already establish the long-term pattern
indications that can guide further investigation
records that cannot provide useful evidence
activity.explanation: The researchers retain the photographs but seek consistent observations. “Clues” preserves their limited value without treating them as either proof or useless records.

evidence.title: A Lake’s Early Ice
evidence.context: The group retained the photographs as clues but turned to daily temperature records and a consistent series of shoreline observations. It wanted to understand a pattern across winters, rather than treating one striking comparison as the pattern itself. Photographs could direct an investigation without completing it.

sections.heading: Read the local meaning before recalling the dictionary
body: Before looking at choices, replace the word with a plain phrase. “Guarded wording” in a cautious report means wording that avoids a strong claim.
Substitute each candidate into the sentence. Keep the grammar, meaning, and tone of the original.

examples.text:
Mara had expected her grandmother’s desk to contain something impressive: the letters of a celebrated traveler, perhaps, or the plans for a house never built. Instead she found grocery lists. Dates ran across the tops in an increasingly uneven hand. Beside “pears,” on one list, her grandmother had written “Mara likes the green ones.”

Her brother suggested recycling the papers. The desk was going to a neighbor, and neither of them wanted another box in an already crowded apartment. Mara agreed that they could not preserve everything. She set aside the advertisements, the duplicate receipts, and three envelopes that held nothing. But she slipped the pear list into her coat pocket.

On the way home she stopped at the corner shop. For years she had bought whichever fruit cost least, making purchases as efficiently as possible. That evening she stood before the pears longer than she needed to. The green ones were not on sale. She chose two anyway, then laughed at herself for expecting them to taste different. When she reached home, she placed the list beside the fruit rather than filing it away.

Question: As used in “filing it away,” “filing” most nearly means:

Supported answer: putting it into organized storage

Reason: The contrast is between leaving the list visible and storing it among papers. The supported answer is “putting it into organized storage.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.
examples.label: Worked example 1: The Last Drawer

activity.prompt: What does weighing mean here?
activity.explanation: Substitute each meaning into “After weighing the costs.” The committee considers the costs before choosing a trial; it is not necessarily calculating an exact total or changing the expenses. The phrase describes evaluation leading to a decision.
activity.evidenceText: After weighing the costs, the committee chose a modest trial.

questions.subject: reading
questions.questionText: As used in “the handbook prescribed obedience,” “prescribed” most nearly means:
choices: laid down as a required standard
questions.explanation: The introduction tells apprentices what they should do, expressing a normative requirement. It does not predict or document compliance, and the medical sense does not fit the instruction context.

passage.title: The Apprentices’ Margins
passage.context:
The printer’s handbook of 1792 contains a stern introduction: an apprentice should follow the master’s method exactly, for variation produces waste. For a historian interested in how printing was taught, the sentence seems to promise a simple hierarchy. The master possesses knowledge; the apprentice receives it. Three surviving copies, however, complicate that arrangement.

In one copy, a reader has written an alternative way to set a difficult line of type. A master might have written the alternative method, and an apprentice might have copied it without ever using it. The surviving copies were retained by workshops that later became collections; unmarked or heavily damaged copies may have disappeared. The historian cannot infer how typical these readers were simply from their survival.

The handbook prescribed obedience; the marked copies preserve acts of judgment. These are not mutually exclusive facts. They belong to different kinds of evidence: one states an ideal of instruction, while the others show several encounters with the instructions.

reviewQuestions.subject: reading
reviewQuestions.questionText: Which situation best illustrates Passage B’s concern?
choices: A model fails to print the name of the famous storm on a citywide map
Two forecasts use different colors while predicting the same local flood boundary
Two model versions differ slightly in a citywide total but place a care home’s access road on different sides of the flood boundary
A model uses the same settings on a storm outside the adjustment set
reviewQuestions.explanation: B’s explicit example concerns a small aggregate error with a consequential local effect. Testing unchanged settings illustrates A’s criterion; labels and colors without prediction changes do not capture B’s action-relevant uncertainty.

passage.title: Two Ways to Trust a Flood Model
passage.context:
Passage A — Model developer
We should not judge the new flood model solely by how closely it reproduces one famous storm. A model can be adjusted until it fits a single event beautifully and still fail under different rainfall patterns. We tested the same settings against several earlier storms that had not been used in adjustment. The results were imperfect but generally captured which districts flooded first. I would publish those comparisons and their errors. A visible error range is more useful for planning than an exact-looking line whose reliability has been demonstrated only where it was tuned.

Passage B — Emergency planner
Testing against unused storms is necessary, but a model’s usefulness also depends on the decision being made. An error that barely changes a citywide total can move a predicted flood boundary across a care home’s access road. For evacuation planning, I need to see how plausible changes in the inputs alter that local prediction. If several reasonable versions disagree, the disagreement itself may justify preparing an alternative route. I am not asking the developer to hide uncertainty in a single worst-case map. I am asking for uncertainty to be expressed where it can change an action.

The model estimates flood extent from rainfall, ground conditions, and drainage information. Neither writer claims that earlier storms cover every future possibility. Both support making limits visible rather than presenting one unqualified forecast.

reviewQuestions.subject: reading
reviewQuestions.questionText: In “served more households in absolute terms,” “absolute” most nearly means:
choices: expressed as a count rather than a share
free from all possible measurement error
reviewQuestions.explanation: The contrast is between a larger number of visiting households and a smaller percentage of a larger population. “Absolute” refers to the count, not guaranteed precision, permanence, or the absence of a defined service area.

passage.title: A Changing Denominator
passage.context:
A city’s annual report announced that use of its neighborhood advice centers had increased. The statement was true in one sense: the centers recorded more visits. The report also said that “a growing proportion of local households is receiving help.” That second claim required information the visit totals did not supply.

The accompanying table separates visits, distinct households recorded as visiting, and households estimated to live in the service area. Staff assigned each visiting household an anonymous identifier, so repeat visits could be distinguished from first visits within a year. The identifiers were reset at the start of the next year, meaning the table could not show which households returned from one year to the next.

A researcher, Oren, noted that the share of households recorded as visiting had actually declined, even though both visits and distinct visiting households had risen. New housing had expanded the estimated service-area population more rapidly. The centers had served more households in absolute terms while reaching a smaller share of the enlarged population.

This did not establish that residents found the service less helpful. The table included no measure of satisfaction, whether a problem was resolved, or how many households needed advice. Nor did it show that any specific household had lost access. Oren recommended keeping the original statement about visits, replacing the proportional claim, and adding a separate study of unmet need. “The denominator is not an inconvenience,” he wrote. “It is part of the question.” The revised report retained all three columns rather than choosing the one that made the largest increase appear.

blocks.title: Evidence-based inference: Use the contradiction test on tempting options

lesson.title: Evidence-based inference
lesson.intro: Use clues in the passage to reach a supported conclusion.

sections.heading: Use the contradiction test on tempting options
body: For each remaining choice, ask what would have to be true. Then look for a passage detail that supports or contradicts that requirement.
Approving another trial does not promise permanent service. A choice that preserves uncertainty can fit better than one that sounds decisive.

examples.text:
Nico spent the first morning of the sound workshop recording traffic. The instructor asked him to choose a location and listen there for ten minutes before touching the recorder. He picked the bridge because he knew what he would hear: engines, tires, horns. He pressed the recording button after less than a minute.

When the instructor played his clip, the traffic filled every second. “You found what you expected,” she said. She sent him back without suggesting a different location. This time Nico stayed under the bridge. He noticed water striking a loose piece of timber, a bicycle chain clicking above him, and pauses in which the river seemed louder than the road. He began recording only after the ten minutes had passed.

That afternoon he compared the clips. The second still contained engines; listening had not removed them. But it also held the soft intervals he had missed. He labeled the first file “Bridge” and hesitated over the second. Finally he gave both files the same name and added only the dates. The place had not changed enough to explain the difference.

Question: Why does Nico give both files the same place name?

Supported answer: He recognizes that his attention, rather than a different location, explains the contrast

Reason: The last sentence states that the place had not changed enough to explain the difference. The supported answer is “He recognizes that his attention, rather than a different location, explains the contrast.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.
examples.label: Worked example 4: Listening Beneath the Bridge

activity.prompt: The text says, “Some residents welcomed the change; others remained skeptical.” Which inference fails the contradiction test?
activity.explanation: “Others remained skeptical” directly conflicts with universal support. Use explicit counterevidence to eliminate an attractive overstatement.

sections.heading: Pace a decision instead of rereading everything
body: Link a clue to your conclusion: “The text says __, so I can reasonably conclude __.” The better answer should require fewer details you have to invent.
If neither choice has a clear link, return to the relevant action or contrast instead of inventing an explanation.

activity.prompt: Which detail most directly supports the inference that the coach accepts Leah’s different portrayal of him?
choices: He mentions championships when Leah asks
The trophy cabinet appears at the far edge
He asks to keep the pencil lines around the unfinished tile
activity.explanation: His request retains the portrait’s focus on work rather than trophies. It is an action supporting acceptance; his earlier comment about the cabinet expresses a reservation.

evidence.title: The Unfinished Portrait
evidence.context:
Leah asked him instead to keep working while she made several sketches. He told her about a student who had returned years later to say that the team had been the first place she felt useful. He mentioned championships only when Leah asked. Her sketches showed his hands above the tile, one hand steadying it while the other tested the corner.

In the finished portrait, the trophy cabinet appeared at the far edge. The coach objected mildly that anyone looking for the championship would have to search. Leah said that anyone looking for him would not. The coach considered the canvas, then asked whether she could leave the pencil lines around the unfinished tile visible. She had planned to cover them. She agreed to let them remain.

sections.heading: Review the reason for the miss and test the repair
body: After a miss, name the unsupported leap: motive, certainty, future outcome, or a claim about everyone.
Replace it with a smaller conclusion and cite the action or statement that supports it. Try the same process on new text.

activity.prompt: An inference says Luis now finds the front entrance useless. What is the smallest supported correction?
choices: He values the side path’s encounters while still using the front steps for quick errands
He chooses the side path because it has become the quicker route
He uses the side path only when his father needs a route without steps
activity.explanation: The paragraph explicitly keeps the front entrance useful and the side path longer. Luis sometimes chooses the side path alone because his experience of it has changed.

evidence.title: The Second Entrance
evidence.context: When his father recovered, Luis used the front steps again for quick errands. But he sometimes chose the side path alone. It had not become shorter, and the front entrance had not become less useful. The route he had called inconvenient now held encounters he would otherwise have missed. He stopped referring to the doors as the usual entrance and the other one.

lesson.title: Algebra
lesson.intro: Solve equations and inequalities, then check that your answer fits.

sections.heading: Equations: isolate, then verify
body: First multiply the number outside parentheses by every term inside. Then combine matching terms. With two equations, add or subtract them to remove a variable (elimination). If a variable is already alone, replace it in the other equation (substitution).
Worked example: 4(x − 2) = 2x + 10 becomes 4x − 8 = 2x + 10, so x = 9. Verify: both original sides equal 28. For x + y = 11 and x − y = 3, adding gives 2x = 14, so x = 7 and y = 4.
sections.tip: Before filling a bubble, reread whether the question asks for x, y, a sum, or a product.

examples.label: Fast verification
examples.text: Substitute your final candidate into the original equation, not just the simplified equation.

activity.prompt: 6(x − 3) = 2x + 10. What is the left side after distribution?
activity.explanation: Multiply both terms in the parentheses by 6: 6x−18. The first wrong choice multiplies only x; the last changes the sign of the constant. The resulting equation is 6x−18=2x+10.

questions.subject: math
questions.questionText: What is \(x + y\)?
questions.explanation: The second equation gives \(x = y + 1\). Substitute into the first: \(2(y + 1) + 3y = 17\), so \(5y = 15\) and \(y = 3\). Then \(x = 4\) and \(x + y = 7\). A trap is stopping at x or y instead of answering the requested sum.

questions.subject: math
questions.questionText: What is xy?
questions.explanation: From the second equation, \(y = 2x - 1\). Substitute: \(3x + 2(2x - 1) = 19\), so \(7x = 21\) and \(x = 3\). Then \(y = 5\) and \(xy = 15\). The question requests the product, not either variable or their sum.

lesson.title: Algebra
lesson.intro: Solve equations and inequalities, then check that your answer fits.

sections.heading: Restrictions and multiple branches
body: First rule out values that make a denominator—the bottom of a fraction—zero. Absolute value measures distance from zero, so the inside may be positive or negative. Check both possibilities. After squaring, test each possible answer in the original equation.
Worked example: \(\frac{x^2-16}{x-4}=10\) has x ≠ 4. Cancel (x − 4) to obtain x + 4 = 10, so x = 6. For |3x + 1| = 8, solve 3x + 1 = 8 and 3x + 1 = −8, giving x = 7/3 or x = −3.

For an absolute-value inequality \(|u|<a\) with \(a>0\), use \(-a<u<a\); ≤ includes endpoints. For \(|u|>a\), use \(u<-a\) or \(u>a\). Example: \(|x-4|<3\) gives \(-3<x-4<3\), so \(1<x<7\). A less-than inequality describes the numbers between its two ends.
sections.tip: A canceled factor keeps its original domain restriction.

examples.label: Keep both branches
examples.text: |A| = b with b > 0 means A = b or A = −b; with b < 0 there is no solution.

activity.prompt: What is the complete set of real solutions to x²=36?
activity.explanation: Both −6 and 6 square to 36. The square-root symbol √36 denotes the principal root 6, but solving x²=36 requires both signs. Using ±36 fails to undo the squaring.

sections.heading: Quadratics and inequalities
body: Try writing the quadratic (an expression whose highest power is 2) as multiplied pieces, called factors. Otherwise use the quadratic formula or rewrite it as a squared expression. If you multiply or divide an inequality by a negative, reverse its sign.

Worked example: x² − 8x + 15 = (x − 3)(x − 5), so its zeros are 3 and 5. The product is negative between the zeros and positive outside. Thus x² − 8x + 15 < 0 has 3 < x < 5; strict inequalities exclude the zeros.

When factoring is awkward, use the quadratic formula: for \(ax^2+bx+c=0\), \(x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}\), with \(a\ne0\). Discriminant \(D=b^2-4ac\) gives two real roots if positive, one repeated real root if zero, and no real roots if negative. Example: \(x^2-4x-1=0\) gives \(x=2\pm\sqrt5\). Completing the square gives the same roots: \((x-2)^2=5\).
sections.tip: Test a point from each interval when the expression’s sign is uncertain.

examples.label: Cross-term check
examples.text: (x + y)² = x² + 2xy + y². Never drop the 2xy term.

activity.prompt: (x − 4)(x + 1) > 0. Which intervals work?
activity.explanation: The factors have the same sign below −1 and above 4, making the product positive. Between the roots their signs differ. The strict inequality excludes the roots; the inclusive outside intervals would also admit a zero product.

sections.heading: Rational and radical equations: protect the original statement
body: Rule out values that make any denominator zero. Cancel whole multiplied pieces, never individual terms joined by + or −. The expression inside a square root must be zero or positive. Anything equal to that square root must also be zero or positive.

Worked example: \(\sqrt{x+12}=x\) gives x ≥ 0. Squaring produces x² − x − 12 = 0, so candidates are 4 and −3. Substitution accepts 4 because √16 = 4, but rejects −3 because √9 = 3. For \(\frac1{x-2}=\frac2{x+1}\), exclude 2 and −1; then x + 1 = 2x − 4 gives x = 5, which is valid.

Test each possible answer in the original equation before counting, adding, or listing solutions. For an inequality with fractions, mark where the top or bottom becomes zero. Test one number between each pair of marks to find the sign.

Use a common denominator before canceling. For nonzero a and b, \(\frac1a+\frac1b=\frac{a+b}{ab}\) and \(\frac1a-\frac1b=\frac{b-a}{ab}\). Their quotient is \(\frac{a+b}{b-a}\), requiring \(a\ne b\). Cancel the common factor ab only after forming the quotient.
sections.tip: A zero denominator is an excluded boundary, even when a factor cancels later.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: \(\frac{x^2-1}{x-1}=2\) simplifies to x + 1 = 2, but its candidate x = 1 is excluded, so the original equation has no solution.

activity.prompt: (x² − 1)/(x − 1) = 3 simplifies to x + 1 = 3. What restriction survives cancellation?
activity.explanation: The original denominator cannot be zero. Cancellation does not put the excluded input back into the domain.

questions.subject: math
questions.stem: a and b are nonzero real numbers, with \(a \ne  b\).
questions.questionText: Which expression equals \(\frac{\frac1a+\frac1b}{\frac1a-\frac1b}\)?
questions.explanation: Put each part over the common denominator ab. The numerator becomes \(\frac{a+b}{ab}\) and the denominator becomes \(\frac{b-a}{ab}\). Dividing cancels ab and gives \(\frac{a+b}{b-a}\). The order \(b - a\) comes from \(\frac1a-\frac1b\); reversing it changes the sign.

reviewQuestions.subject: math
reviewQuestions.questionText: What is x?
reviewQuestions.explanation: Multiply every term by \(12: 3(x + 3) - 2(x - 1) = 24\). Distribute the subtraction to get \(3x + 9 - 2x + 2 = 24\), so \(x = 13\). Substitution gives \(4 - 2 = 2\). The common trap is changing \(-2(x - 1)\) to \(-2x - 2\).

reviewQuestions.subject: math
reviewQuestions.questionText: Which value satisfies the equation?
reviewQuestions.explanation: A square root is nonnegative, so \(x \ge  0\). Squaring gives \(2x + 3 = x^{2}\), or \((x - 3)(x + 1) = 0\). The candidates are 3 and \(-1\), but only 3 is nonnegative and satisfies the original equation. Squaring introduces the extraneous candidate \(-1\).

lesson.title: Algebra
lesson.intro: Solve equations and inequalities, then check that your answer fits.

sections.heading: Equations: isolate, then verify
body: First multiply the number outside parentheses by every term inside. Then combine matching terms. With two equations, add or subtract them to remove a variable (elimination). If a variable is already alone, replace it in the other equation (substitution).
Worked example: 4(x − 2) = 2x + 10 becomes 4x − 8 = 2x + 10, so x = 9. Verify: both original sides equal 28. For x + y = 11 and x − y = 3, adding gives 2x = 14, so x = 7 and y = 4.
sections.tip: Before filling a bubble, reread whether the question asks for x, y, a sum, or a product.

examples.label: Fast verification
examples.text: Substitute your final candidate into the original equation, not just the simplified equation.

activity.prompt: 6(x − 3) = 2x + 10. What is the left side after distribution?
activity.explanation: Multiply both terms in the parentheses by 6: 6x−18. The first wrong choice multiplies only x; the last changes the sign of the constant. The resulting equation is 6x−18=2x+10.

questions.subject: math
questions.questionText: What is \(x + y\)?
questions.explanation: The second equation gives \(x = y + 1\). Substitute into the first: \(2(y + 1) + 3y = 17\), so \(5y = 15\) and \(y = 3\). Then \(x = 4\) and \(x + y = 7\). A trap is stopping at x or y instead of answering the requested sum.

questions.subject: math
questions.questionText: What is xy?
questions.explanation: From the second equation, \(y = 2x - 1\). Substitute: \(3x + 2(2x - 1) = 19\), so \(7x = 21\) and \(x = 3\). Then \(y = 5\) and \(xy = 15\). The question requests the product, not either variable or their sum.

sections.heading: Locate the quantity and unit
body: Name the quantity requested, its unit, and the treatment or time. Match the table column or graph axis before comparing values. In a graph, use the legend to select the correct series.
A final amount, a change, and a rate answer different questions. Reading the largest number without its label can select the wrong quantity.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For the lowest outlet dust, compare 6, 3, and 9 mg/m³: choose Vent Y. Its 45 m³/min airflow answers a different question.

activity.prompt: A thermometer table lists elapsed time and temperature. Which column answers “how warm at 4 min”?
activity.explanation: The question asks for temperature at a specified time. Time selects the row; temperature is the requested output.
activity.evidenceText: Trial 1: at 4 min the sample is 32°C and has volume 50 mL.

evidence.title: Locate the quantity and unit

sections.heading: Distinguish totals, changes, and fractions
body: Change = final − initial. Amount removed = initial − final. Fraction removed divides the removed amount by the initial amount; fraction remaining divides the final amount by the initial amount.

examples.label: Worked example

The unknown definitely contains only C and E because its bands match their retention factors.

sections.heading: Check simultaneous constraints
body: Turn every requirement into a separate test. “At least” includes equality; “greater than” does not. Eliminate a candidate as soon as it fails a required condition.
Write ratios in the requested direction. Output per area means output/area. Reversing numerator and denominator changes both the units and the ranking.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: Need airflow ≥70 m³/min and outlet dust ≤7 mg/m³. X passes both (80, 6); Y fails airflow; Z fails dust.

activity.prompt: Which water sample meets BOTH temperature below 25°C and oxygen at least 6 mg/L?
activity.explanation: M has 24°C and 6 mg/L and passes both. N fails the strict temperature limit; O fails the oxygen minimum.

evidence.title: Check simultaneous constraints
evidence.context: Use the same three air filters; the specification requires both sufficient airflow and sufficiently low outlet dust.

sections.heading: Normalize unequal sample sizes
body: Counts measure totals; densities measure counts per area or volume. Divide before ranking samples of unequal sizes. If every sample has the same size, counts and densities rank them alike.
A percentage needs its own denominator. Percent germinated uses all starting seeds; mean root length might include only seedlings that sprouted. Read the study definition.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: Quadrat A: 36/6 = 6 plants/m². B: 45/15 = 3 plants/m². B has the larger count, but A has the greater density.

activity.prompt: Which pool has the greater insect density?

lesson.title: Sentence Structure
lesson.intro: Build complete sentences and join their ideas correctly.

sections.heading: Clauses and phrases
body: A clause has a subject (who or what it is about) and a verb (an action or state, such as runs or is). An independent clause is a complete thought that can stand alone. A dependent clause needs another clause to finish its thought; it often starts with because, although, if, when, or while.

A phrase is a group of words without a complete subject and verb. Find those two parts first. If removing a starter such as because leaves a complete thought, you had a dependent clause. Do not decide only by where you pause.

examples.text: The excited child opened his present.
examples.label: Independent clause — you can stop here

examples.text: When the excited child opened his present…
examples.label: Dependent clause — the opening word forces you to keep going

examples.text: Excited to open his present…
examples.label: Phrase — no subject doing the action

sections.tip: Read it aloud. If you can stop talking, it is an independent clause. If you feel forced to keep going, it is dependent or a phrase.

questions.stem: Although the museum closes at six
questions.questionText: What kind of word group is this?
questions.explanation: “The museum” is the subject and “closes” is the verb. “Although” makes the thought dependent: we still need the main statement. Without “Although,” “The museum closes at six” can stand alone.
questions.subject: english

questions.questionText: Which word group is a phrase rather than a clause?
questions.explanation: “Near the old stone bridge” has no subject performing a verb. The other three groups each contain a subject and a verb; “While the river rose” is a dependent clause.
questions.subject: english

questions.stem: Even though the trail was muddy
questions.questionText: Which change makes this word group an independent clause?
questions.explanation: Removing the entire two-word starter “Even though” leaves “The trail was muddy,” a complete thought with subject “trail” and verb “was.” Removing the subject or the verb does not create an independent clause.
questions.subject: english

questions.questionText: Which word group is a dependent clause?
choices: Before the crew repaired the roof
questions.explanation: “Before” makes “the crew repaired the roof” dependent. It supplies a subject and working verb but leaves the reader waiting for a main statement. The first choice is independent; the other two are phrases.
questions.subject: english

lesson.title: Sentence Structure
lesson.intro: Build complete sentences and join their ideas correctly.

sections.heading: Sentence fragments
body: Read the entire sentence. It needs a subject, a main verb, and a complete thought; a fragment is missing one of these.
“The student running to class” has no main verb. Add one: “The student running to class dropped her bottle.” An -ed form can be either a past-tense verb or a modifier, so check its job.

examples.text: My little brother Shaun is excited to go to the beach and surf.
examples.label: Complete — has a subject and a working verb

examples.text: Excited to go to the beach and surf.
examples.label: Fragment — no subject

sections.tip: An -ing form needs a helping verb to serve as the main verb. An -ed form may be a past-tense verb or a modifier; check its job in the complete sentence.

questions.stem: The athlete training before sunrise.
questions.questionText: Which revision makes a complete sentence?
choices: The athlete to train before sunrise
questions.explanation: “Trained” supplies a working main verb for the subject “athlete.” “Training” and “to train” do not work as the main verb in these choices. The phrase “Training before sunrise” also lacks a subject.
questions.subject: english

questions.stem: The sculpture standing in the courtyard.
questions.questionText: Which revision supplies a working main verb?
choices: The sculpture standing in the courtyard
The sculpture standing in the courtyard attracts visitors
